citation.title: Philanthrolateralism: Private Funding and Corporate Influence in the United Nations
citation.venue_or_publisher: Global Policy, Vol. 8, Supplement 5 (Wiley / University of Durham)
citation.type: journal article (special issue, short policy-oriented article)

question: How private funding from corporations and philanthropic foundations, and UN-business partnerships, change UN governance and give corporate actors influence. The article does not address UNFCCC delegations or badges.
data: No original dataset. It draws on secondary figures: UN Secretary-General reports (2013 voluntary contributions), UN Women, UNDP and WHO funding reports, OECD, Gates Foundation and Coca-Cola reports, and corporate and partnership websites. Periods are mostly 2010-2016.
method: Descriptive and argumentative policy analysis with illustrative examples (Coca-Cola, L'Oreal, Shell, the Gates Foundation, the UN Foundation). No classification scheme or counting procedure is described.

definitions.definition: A shift from inclusive multilateral decision-making within the UN to global club governance in exclusive partnerships.
definitions.quote: the shift from inclusive multilateral decision-making within the UN to global club governance in exclusive partnerships – or what we call a shift towards ‘philanthrolateralism’

definitions.definition: Applying business and market-based approaches to development, with an emphasis on short-term results. The authors give no formal definition; this is how they describe it.
definitions.quote: applying a business model to the measurement of results

definitions.definition: Used for the growing share of non-core, earmarked funding. Not defined formally; the authors link it to non-core contributions and earmarked trust funds.
definitions.quote: overcome ‘minilateralism’ by reducing the share of non-core contributions and earmarked trust funds in UN finance

proxies.indicator: Specified voluntary contributions from foundations, corporations and civil society, as reported by the UN and by individual agencies
proxies.quote: specified voluntary contributions from foundations, corporations and civil society to the UN system amounted to about US$3.3 billion, or 14 per cent

proxies.indicator: Corporate executives holding seats on partnership boards or advisory councils (for example the Shell chairman chairing the SEforAll Administrative Board)
proxies.quote: Charles Holliday, Chairman of Royal Dutch Shell, for instance, is chair of the Administrative Board of SEforAll

proxies.indicator: Direct grant-making, placement of foundation staff in decision-making bodies, board seats on global funds, and matching funds
proxies.quote: through the placement of Foundation staff in decision-making bodies of international organizations and global partnerships

findings.claim: Total private funding of the UN is hard to track because it is mostly extra-budgetary. It was about 14% of specified voluntary contributions in 2013.
findings.quote: tracking the total volume of private contributions to the UN Secretariat and the UN system is difficult and cumbersome

findings.claim: Direct corporate funding is small relative to the attention it receives (UN Women 1.8% in 2015; UNDP about 3% in 2010-2015).
findings.quote: the quantity of direct funding from corporations to the UN system and to global partnerships has remained surprisingly low

findings.claim: Partnerships are cheap for companies and bring image benefits. The authors raise the risk to UN neutrality.
findings.quote: Partnerships with the UN are a cheap bargain for private companies.

findings.claim: UN partnerships lack disclosure requirements, conflict-of-interest rules and accountability standards.
findings.quote: UN partnerships have very limited public disclosure requirements if any, and conflict of interest regulations and accountability standards are not in place

findings.claim: Corporate actors sit in the governance of global partnerships even though they supply a small share of the money (private companies were 2.7% of EWEC financial commitments).
findings.quote: corporate actors are systematically involved in the decision-making structures of these partnerships

findings.claim: Authors' recommendation (not a finding): governments should reconsider the unconditioned opening of the UN to business and corporate philanthropy.
findings.quote: reconsider the often unconditioned opening of the UN to the business sector and corporate philanthropy

limitations.point: Disaggregated system-wide data on corporate funding to the UN are not available.
limitations.quote: Disaggregated system-wide information on the quality and quantity of funding from the corporate sector is not available.

limitations.point: Global data on philanthropic contributions to development are not systematically collected.
limitations.quote: Global data on philanthropic contributions dedicated to international development causes is not systematically collected.

limitations.point: Not authors' statements: the article is short and non-systematic, with no stated method. It does not cover UNFCCC, delegates, badges or fossil fuel links. It is advocacy-oriented, from an NGO think tank.
